html:
The Sámi are the native people of Sápmi, the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia's Kola Peninsula. The map shows them under this name at times from 200 to 1530, and as "Sami" in 900; the earlier label Saami covers their ancient history.

In these centuries the Sámi lived by hunting wild reindeer, fishing, sealing on the coast and trapping furs. Families moved between seasonal camps in groups called siida, each with its own lands. Their religion centred on the spirits of nature and on the noaidi, a shaman who traveled to the spirit world to the beat of a drum. Some Sámi kept a few tame reindeer for milk and transport; large-scale reindeer herding developed later, mostly from the 1500s and 1600s.

Their neighbours wanted their furs. Around 890 a Norwegian chieftain, Ohthere, told King Alfred the Great of England that he took tribute from the Sámi in furs, feathers, whalebone and ship ropes of walrus and seal hide. Norse and Sámi traded and sometimes intermarried in the Viking Age. Later three states taxed them: Norway, Sweden and Novgorod, whose claims overlapped in the north, so many Sámi paid tax to more than one ruler. In Sweden, merchants called birkarls held the right to trade with and tax them.

After 1530 kings pushed harder into the north. They built churches, encouraged settlers and set out to convert the Sámi, and many noaidi drums were seized and burned.
